intro: You already make one part of a word strong (TEA-cher) and say small words quickly (can → 'kən'). Now we move to whole sentences: which words are strong, how words join together (turn off → 'tur-noff'), and how to keep the English beat. Say every sentence out loud and clap along!
teachingNotes: Explain the two terms in plain Indonesian the first time. Content words (kata isi) carry the meaning and are STRESSED (louder, longer, higher): nouns (Rina, bank, rice), main verbs (work, buy, like, have as 'punya'), adjectives (new, hot), question words (what, where, when, who, why, how), not and negative short forms (don't, isn't, can't), and adverbs like today, here, often. Function words (kata tugas) are the small 'glue' words and are WEAK (quick, quiet, often with the weak 'uh' sound from a2-pron-ed-weak-forms): a, an, the, to, of, at, in, on, for, and, but, is/am/are/was, helper do/does, positive can, pronouns (I, you, he, it) and my, your, his, her. Telegram test: keep only the content words and the message still makes sense (RINA WORKS BANK). Inside a long content word only its stressed syllable is strong (com-PU-ter).

Indonesian trap and the node's common error: learners give every word the same strength, like Indonesian, so 'I WANT TO GO TO THE SHOP' sounds robotic and the key words get lost; right: 'I WANT to GO to the SHOP'. Exceptions to name: a small word at the END of a sentence or in a short answer is said in full (Yes, I CAN. Where are you FROM?); negatives are always strong (I CAN'T COME). Don't teach contrastive or emphatic stress (moving stress to change meaning) or intonation: that comes later.

Linking (only consonant → vowel here): when a word ends in a consonant SOUND and the next word starts with a vowel SOUND, the consonant moves over to the next word with no pause: turn_off 'tur-noff', an_apple 'a-napple', pick_it_up 'pi-ki-tup', get_up 'ge-tup', look_at 'loo-kat'. It's about sounds, not letters: make_it = 'ma-kit' (the e is silent, the last sound is k); an_hour = 'a-nour' (the h is silent). The -ed ending from a2-past-simple-regular links too: cleaned_it 'clean-dit', worked_on 'work-ton'. Common errors from the node: a stop or pause between the words, 'turn | off', 'an | apple' (Indonesian speakers often put a tiny catch in the throat before a word starting with a vowel). In British English turn off is 'ter-noff' with no r; American English keeps the r: 'tern-off'. Both link.

Listening benefit: linked phrases sound like one word, so learners hear 'come in' as 'coming' or 'look at it' as one long word. Teach them to expect it: 'co-min' = come + in. Don't teach vowel → vowel linking (the small y/w/r sounds in go_out, the_end, far_away), assimilation or dropped sounds: keep to consonant → vowel.

Rhythm: in English the strong beats come at roughly regular times and the weak words between them are squeezed (said faster and weaker). In Indonesian every syllable gets about the same time (sa-ya-mau-ke-pa-sar). Practise by clapping on the strong beats: 'ONE, TWO, THREE' / 'ONE and TWO and THREE' / 'ONE and a TWO and a THREE' all keep 3 claps; 'Rina COOKS RICE' and 'Rina is COOKing the RICE' both have 3 beats. Don't claim the timing is exactly equal: it's a tendency. Checkpoint items ask learners to write the stressed words, the two words that link, or the number of strong beats (accept numbers or words, any capitalisation).

Grammar scope: A0/A1 grammar (be, simple present, present continuous, can, there is, imperatives, was/were) plus positive past simple with regular -ed verbs. No irregular past (went, had), no did/didn't, no will or going to, no present perfect. Phrasal verbs like turn off, pick up, get up are taught as phrases with their Indonesian meaning, not as a grammar topic.

keyPoints.title: Stress the content words
keyPoints.explanation: Content words carry the meaning: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, question words and not (don't, can't). Say them louder, longer and higher. Function words are the small glue words: a, the, to, of, in, at, and, is, I, my. Say them quickly and quietly. Don't give every word the same strength.

examples.en: I want to go to the shop.
examples.id: Saya mau pergi ke toko. (I WANT to GO to the SHOP)
Di mana terminal bus? (WHERE is the BUS STA-tion)
Budi tidak bisa datang hari ini. (BU-di CAN'T COME to-DAY)

id.title: Tekan kata isi
id.explanation: Kata isi (content words) membawa arti: kata benda, kata kerja utama, kata sifat, kata tanya, dan not (don't, can't). Ucapkan lebih keras, lebih panjang dan lebih tinggi. Kata tugas (function words) adalah kata kecil 'perekat': a, the, to, of, in, at, and, is, I, my. Ucapkan cepat dan pelan. Jangan beri semua kata kekuatan yang sama.

keyPoints.title: Link a consonant to the next vowel
keyPoints.explanation: When a word ends in a consonant sound and the next word starts with a vowel sound, join them with no pause: the consonant moves to the next word. turn off = 'tur-noff', an apple = 'a-napple', pick it up = 'pi-ki-tup'. Listen for the sound, not the letter: make it = 'ma-kit' (the e is silent).

id.title: Sambungkan konsonan ke vokal berikutnya
id.explanation: Kalau sebuah kata berakhir dengan bunyi konsonan dan kata berikutnya diawali bunyi vokal, sambungkan tanpa jeda: konsonannya pindah ke kata berikutnya. turn off = 'tur-noff', an apple = 'a-napple', pick it up = 'pi-ki-tup'. Dengarkan bunyinya, bukan hurufnya: make it = 'ma-kit' (huruf e tidak dibaca).

keyPoints.title: Keep the beat
keyPoints.explanation: English has a beat: the strong words come at roughly regular times, and the weak words between them are squeezed in quickly. Indonesian gives every syllable about the same time. Count the strong beats and clap on them: 'Rina COOKS RICE' and 'Rina is COOKing the RICE' both have 3 beats.

examples.en: One and two and three and four.
examples.id: Satu dan dua dan tiga dan empat. (4 ketukan)
Rina sedang memasak nasinya. (3 ketukan: RI-na, COOK, RICE)

id.title: Jaga ketukannya
id.explanation: Bahasa Inggris punya ketukan: kata-kata kuat datang dengan jarak yang kurang lebih teratur, dan kata-kata lemah di antaranya diselipkan dengan cepat. Bahasa Indonesia memberi setiap suku kata waktu yang kira-kira sama. Hitung ketukan kuatnya dan tepuk tangan di situ: 'Rina COOKS RICE' dan 'Rina is COOKing the RICE' sama-sama punya 3 ketukan.

assessment.rubric: Correct: lives in (the s/z sound of lives moves to in: 'liv-zin'). 'Budi lives' = 0 (Budi ends in a vowel and lives starts with a consonant). 'in Medan' = 0 (n + m, two consonants).

assessment.rubric: Correct: 4 (DI-mas, CLEANS, KIT-chen, SUN-day; the and on are squeezed in). 6 (every word) = 0. 3 or 5 = 0.

assessment.prompt: Which sentence has the same number of strong beats as 'Sari reads books'? A: Sari is reading a book. B: Sari reads books at night. Write A or B.
assessment.rubric: Correct: A (SA-ri, READ-ing, BOOK = 3 beats, like SA-ri READS BOOKS; is and a are squeezed in). B has 4 beats (Sari, reads, books, night) = 0.

blocks.text:
In A1 you learnt **word stress**: one syllable of a word is strong (**TEA-cher**). Sentences work the same way: some **words** are strong and some are weak.

**Content words** are the words that carry the meaning. They are **stressed**: louder, longer and a little higher.
- **nouns** (names of people, places, things): *Rina, bank, rice*
- **main verbs** (the action): *work, buy, like, eat*
- **adjectives** (words that describe): *new, hot, big*
- **question words**: *what, where, when, who, why, how*
- **not** and its short forms: *don't, isn't, can't*
- words like *today, here, often*

**Function words** are the small 'glue' words that hold the sentence together. They are **weak**: quick and quiet, often with the weak 'uh' sound you learnt last time (*to* → 'tə', *can* → 'kən').
- *a, an, the*
- *to, of, at, in, on, for, and, but*
- *is, am, are, was* and *can* (in positive sentences)
- *I, you, he, she, it, we, they* and *my, your, his, her*

**The telegram test:** keep only the content words and the message still makes sense: *RINA · WORKS · BANK*. That's why these words must be clear.

**The Indonesian trap:** in Indonesian we say every word with about the same strength. In English that sounds flat and robotic, and the important words get lost: not *I WANT TO GO TO THE SHOP*, but *I WANT to GO to the SHOP*.

**Two things that seem to break the rule:**
- A small word at the **end** of a sentence, or in a short answer, is said in full: *Yes, I **can**.* *Where are you **from**?* There's nothing after it to lean on.
- **can** is weak, but **can't** is always strong: *I can SWIM* ('kən') vs *I CAN'T SWIM*. The 'not' is the important news.

id.text:
Di A1 kamu sudah belajar **tekanan kata**: satu suku kata di sebuah kata itu kuat (**TEA-cher**). Kalimat juga begitu: ada **kata** yang kuat dan ada yang lemah.

**Kata isi** (content words) adalah kata yang membawa arti. Kata-kata ini **ditekan**: lebih keras, lebih panjang dan sedikit lebih tinggi.
- **kata benda** (nama orang, tempat, benda): *Rina, bank, rice*
- **kata kerja utama** (kegiatannya): *work, buy, like, eat*
- **kata sifat** (kata yang menjelaskan): *new, hot, big*
- **kata tanya**: *what, where, when, who, why, how*
- **not** dan bentuk pendeknya: *don't, isn't, can't*
- kata seperti *today, here, often*

**Kata tugas** (function words) adalah kata-kata kecil 'perekat' yang menyatukan kalimat. Kata-kata ini **lemah**: cepat dan pelan, sering dengan bunyi 'e' lemah yang kamu pelajari sebelumnya (*to* → 'te', *can* → 'ken').
- *a, an, the*
- *to, of, at, in, on, for, and, but*
- *is, am, are, was* dan *can* (di kalimat positif)
- *I, you, he, she, it, we, they* dan *my, your, his, her*

**Tes telegram:** sisakan kata isinya saja, dan pesannya tetap bisa dipahami: *RINA · WORKS · BANK* (Rina · kerja · bank). Karena itulah kata-kata ini harus jelas.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** dalam bahasa Indonesia kita mengucapkan setiap kata dengan kekuatan yang kira-kira sama. Dalam bahasa Inggris itu terdengar datar seperti robot, dan kata-kata pentingnya hilang: bukan *I WANT TO GO TO THE SHOP*, tapi *I WANT to GO to the SHOP*.

**Dua hal yang kelihatannya melanggar aturan:**
- Kata kecil di **akhir** kalimat, atau di jawaban pendek, diucapkan utuh: *Yes, I **can**.* *Where are you **from**?* Tidak ada kata sesudahnya untuk disandari.
- **can** itu lemah, tapi **can't** selalu kuat: *I can SWIM* ('ken') vs *I CAN'T SWIM*. Kata 'tidak' adalah berita pentingnya.

blocks.text:
English speakers don't stop between words. When a word **ends in a consonant sound** and the next word **starts with a vowel sound**, the consonant moves over to the next word. We call this **linking**.

(A **consonant** is a 'huruf mati' sound like n, k, t, s. A **vowel** is a 'huruf hidup' sound like a, e, i, o, u.)
- *turn off* → 'tur-**noff**'
- *an apple* → 'a-**napple**'
- *pick it up* → 'pi-**ki**-**tup**'
- *get up* → 'ge-**tup**'

**Listen to the sound, not the letter.** Two examples that seem to break the rule:
- *make it* → 'ma-**kit**'. *make* ends with the letter e, but the e is silent: the last **sound** is k, so it links.
- *an hour* → 'a-**nour**'. *hour* starts with the letter h, but the h is silent: the first **sound** is a vowel, so *an* links to it.

The **-ed** ending from the past simple links too: *I cleaned it* → 'clean-**dit**', *We worked on it* → 'work-**to**-**nit**'. Say the -ed clearly and let it move.

**The Indonesian trap:** in Indonesian we often put a tiny stop in the throat before a word that starts with a vowel. In English that stop makes speech sound choppy: not *an | apple*, *turn | off*, but *a-napple*, *tur-noff*.

**Why it helps you listen:** linked words sound like one word. *Come in* sounds like 'co-min' (almost *coming*), *look at it* sounds like 'loo-ka-tit'. When you know this, you can hear the words inside.

British English says *turn off* without the r: 'ter-noff'. American English keeps the r: 'tern-off'. Both link.

id.text:
Penutur bahasa Inggris tidak berhenti di antara kata. Kalau sebuah kata **berakhir dengan bunyi konsonan** dan kata berikutnya **diawali bunyi vokal**, konsonannya pindah ke kata berikutnya. Ini disebut **linking** (menyambung bunyi).

(**Konsonan** = bunyi huruf mati seperti n, k, t, s. **Vokal** = bunyi huruf hidup seperti a, e, i, o, u.)
- *turn off* (matikan) → 'tur-**noff**'
- *an apple* (sebuah apel) → 'a-**napple**'
- *pick it up* (ambil itu) → 'pi-**ki**-**tup**'
- *get up* (bangun) → 'ge-**tup**'

**Dengarkan bunyinya, bukan hurufnya.** Dua contoh yang kelihatannya melanggar aturan:
- *make it* → 'ma-**kit**'. *make* berakhir dengan huruf e, tapi e-nya tidak dibaca: **bunyi** terakhirnya k, jadi tersambung.
- *an hour* → 'a-**nour**'. *hour* diawali huruf h, tapi h-nya tidak dibaca: **bunyi** pertamanya vokal, jadi *an* tersambung ke situ.

Akhiran **-ed** dari past simple juga tersambung: *I cleaned it* → 'clean-**dit**', *We worked on it* → 'work-**to**-**nit**'. Ucapkan -ed dengan jelas dan biarkan pindah ke kata berikutnya.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** dalam bahasa Indonesia kita sering membuat hentakan kecil di tenggorokan sebelum kata yang diawali vokal. Dalam bahasa Inggris hentakan itu membuat ucapan terdengar patah-patah: bukan *an | apple*, *turn | off*, tapi *a-napple*, *tur-noff*.

**Kenapa ini membantu mendengar:** kata-kata yang tersambung terdengar seperti satu kata. *Come in* (masuk) terdengar 'co-min' (hampir seperti *coming*), *look at it* terdengar 'loo-ka-tit'. Kalau kamu tahu ini, kamu bisa mendengar kata-kata di dalamnya.

Bahasa Inggris British mengucapkan *turn off* tanpa r: 'ter-noff'. Bahasa Inggris Amerika tetap membunyikan r: 'tern-off'. Keduanya tetap tersambung.

blocks.text:
Say this in Indonesian: *Sa-ya-mau-ke-pa-sar*. Every syllable gets about the **same time**, like a machine gun: ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta.

English works differently. The **strong** words (the content words) come at roughly **regular** times, like the beats of a song. The **weak** words between them are **squeezed** in: said faster and quieter, so the beat doesn't slow down.

Clap once on each strong word and try it:
- **ONE**, **TWO**, **THREE**, **FOUR**. (4 claps)
- **ONE** and **TWO** and **THREE** and **FOUR**. (still 4 claps)
- **ONE** and a **TWO** and a **THREE** and a **FOUR**. (still 4 claps!)
The sentences get longer, but the claps stay the same. The extra *and* and *a* are squeezed between them.

It's the same in real sentences:
- *RI-na COOKS RICE.* (3 beats)
- *RI-na is COOK-ing the RICE.* (still 3 beats: *is* and *the* are squeezed)

**The Indonesian trap:** giving every word and syllable the same time. Then a short weak word like *the* or *to* becomes as long as *rice*, and the sentence loses its beat.

**How to count beats:** find the content words. Each one is one beat, even a long one: *SU-ra-BA-ya* is one word, so one beat (on its strong syllable).

id.text:
Ucapkan ini dalam bahasa Indonesia: *Sa-ya-mau-ke-pa-sar*. Setiap suku kata mendapat waktu yang **kira-kira sama**, seperti senapan mesin: ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta.

Bahasa Inggris berbeda. Kata-kata **kuat** (kata isi) datang dengan jarak yang kurang lebih **teratur**, seperti ketukan lagu. Kata-kata **lemah** di antaranya **diselipkan**: diucapkan lebih cepat dan lebih pelan, supaya ketukannya tidak melambat.

Tepuk tangan sekali di setiap kata kuat dan coba:
- **ONE**, **TWO**, **THREE**, **FOUR**. (4 tepukan)
- **ONE** and **TWO** and **THREE** and **FOUR**. (tetap 4 tepukan)
- **ONE** and a **TWO** and a **THREE** and a **FOUR**. (tetap 4 tepukan!)
Kalimatnya makin panjang, tapi tepukannya tetap sama. Kata *and* dan *a* tambahan diselipkan di antaranya.

Kalimat sungguhan juga begitu:
- *RI-na COOKS RICE.* (3 ketukan)
- *RI-na is COOK-ing the RICE.* (tetap 3 ketukan: *is* dan *the* diselipkan)

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** memberi setiap kata dan suku kata waktu yang sama. Akibatnya kata lemah yang pendek seperti *the* atau *to* jadi sepanjang *rice*, dan kalimatnya kehilangan ketukan.

**Cara menghitung ketukan:** cari kata isinya. Setiap kata isi = satu ketukan, walaupun panjang: *SU-ra-BA-ya* itu satu kata, jadi satu ketukan (di suku kata kuatnya).

blocks.text:
Let's use all three on one sentence: *Dimas works in an office.*
1. **Find the content words** (strong): *DI-mas*, *WORKS*, *OF-fice*.
2. **Make the rest weak**: *in*, *an* are quick.
3. **Link** consonant to vowel: *works_in_an_office* → 'work-si-na-noffice'.
4. **Keep the beat**: 3 claps, on DI, WORKS and OF.

Result: '**DI**-mas **WORK**-si-na-**NOF**-fice'. It sounds smooth and clear, and the important words stand out.

id.text:
Ayo pakai ketiganya di satu kalimat: *Dimas works in an office.* (Dimas bekerja di sebuah kantor.)
1. **Cari kata isinya** (kuat): *DI-mas*, *WORKS*, *OF-fice*.
2. **Buat sisanya lemah**: *in*, *an* diucapkan cepat.
3. **Sambungkan** konsonan ke vokal: *works_in_an_office* → 'work-si-na-noffice'.
4. **Jaga ketukannya**: 3 tepukan, di DI, WORKS dan OF.

Hasilnya: '**DI**-mas **WORK**-si-na-**NOF**-fice'. Terdengar lancar dan jelas, dan kata-kata pentingnya menonjol.

id.note: SA-ri i-zat HOME: is dan at lemah dan tersambung

suggestedQuestions: How do I know if a word is a content word or a function word?
Why is can weak but can't strong?
How can I hear the words when English speakers link them together?
Why does English sound faster than Indonesian?

flashcards.back: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, question words, not / don't / can't: STRONG
a, an, the, to, of, at, in, and, is, can, I, my: weak and quick

flashcards.front: turn off: how does it sound?
an apple: how does it sound?
make it: make ends in e. Why does it link?
flashcards.back: The e is silent: the last SOUND is k → 'ma-kit'

flashcards.front: can or can't: which one is strong?
flashcards.back: can't (I CAN'T SWIM). can is weak: I can SWIM ('kən')

flashcards.front: ritme bahasa Inggris vs bahasa Indonesia
flashcards.back: English: strong beats at regular times, weak words squeezed. Indonesian: every syllable about the same time.

resources.title: Tim's Pronunciation Workshop: Consonant - vowel linking
resources.note: A short BBC video with the full transcript: Londoners say 'He's holding an egg', and Tim shows how an egg becomes 'anegg'. Then listen and repeat. Some example sentences are above A2 (used to, had to): just listen for the linking.

id.note: Video pendek BBC dengan transkrip lengkap: warga London mengucapkan 'He's holding an egg', dan Tim menunjukkan bagaimana an egg menjadi 'anegg'. Lalu dengarkan dan tirukan. Beberapa contoh kalimatnya di atas level A2 (used to, had to): cukup dengarkan sambungan bunyinya.

id.intro: Kamu sudah bisa membuat satu bagian kata jadi kuat (TEA-cher) dan mengucapkan kata kecil dengan cepat (can → 'ken'). Sekarang kita pindah ke kalimat utuh: kata mana yang kuat, bagaimana kata-kata tersambung (turn off → 'tur-noff'), dan cara menjaga ketukan bahasa Inggris. Ucapkan setiap kalimat dengan suara keras dan tepuk tangan mengikuti ketukannya!
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana aku tahu sebuah kata itu kata isi atau kata tugas?
Kenapa can lemah tapi can't kuat?
Bagaimana aku bisa mendengar kata-katanya kalau penutur bahasa Inggris menyambungnya?
Kenapa bahasa Inggris terdengar lebih cepat daripada bahasa Indonesia?

assessment.sl-1: Tulis kata-kata yang ditekan (kata isi) di kalimat ini: My brother drives a taxi in Bandung.
assessment.sl-2: Sari bilang: 'I don't eat meat.' Apakah kata don't di sini kuat atau lemah? Tulis strong atau weak.
assessment.sl-3: Dua kata mana yang tersambung (konsonan akhir bergabung dengan vokal berikutnya) di: 'Budi lives in Medan.' Tulis kedua kata itu.
assessment.sl-4: Dengarkan. Rina meminta Budi melakukan sesuatu dengan kipas angin. Tulis kata yang kamu dengar sesudah 'turn it': on atau off.
assessment.sl-5: Berapa ketukan kuat di kalimat ini? 'Dimas cleans the kitchen on Sunday.' Tulis angkanya.
assessment.sl-6: Kalimat mana yang jumlah ketukan kuatnya sama dengan 'Sari reads books'? A: Sari is reading a book. B: Sari reads books at night. Tulis A atau B.
